sources.liguori: St Alphonsus Liguori, The Glories of Mary (1888)
sources.faber: Fr Frederick William Faber, The Foot of the Cross (1858)

scripture.text: And they said one to another: Who shall roll us back the stone from the door of the sepulchre?

meditations.body:
Three women walking in the dark, carrying spices for a body,
asking each other the practical question: who shall roll us back the stone?
It is the last worry of the old world.
The problem has been solved since before dawn,
and they will carry it all the way to the garden anyway.
Begin the decade honestly there — with whatever stone you have been
rehearsing the weight of.
You may find the discussion is already obsolete.

scripture.text: And as they were afraid and bowed down their countenance towards the ground, they said unto them: Why seek you the living with the dead? He is not here, but is risen. Remember how he spoke unto you, when he was yet in Galilee,

meditations.body:
Heaven's first Easter word is a question,
and it gently corrects where we look.

scripture.text: For in that he died to sin, he died once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God.

meditations.body:
Notice something in the litanies: of all the mysteries,
the Church calls this one holy — per sanctam resurrectionem tuam.
Why this one, when His birth, His life, His Passion are all holy?
Because holiness has two elements — separation from all that is sin
and weakness, and total belonging to God —
and the Resurrection displays both as nothing before it did.
If the Passion is summed in he humbled himself,
the Resurrection is summed in two words of Paul: vivit Deo.
He liveth unto God. Entirely.
That is what holiness is, and this morning is its portrait.

scripture.text: See my hands and feet, that it is I myself. Handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have.

meditations.body:
List what the mortal years had held:
an infant needing His Mother's milk, a man wearied at the well,
asleep in the storm, hungry, thirsty, afraid in the garden.
After this morning all of it is gone — no fatigue, no need, no infirmity —
and yet it is truly the same body, the Body He received from the Virgin Mary,
the Body that suffered death.
Handle and see.
He eats with them not from hunger but out of merciful condescension.
Glory did not replace the body you know from the Gospels.
It set it free.

scripture.text: When I had a little passed by them, I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him: and I will not let him go, till I bring him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that bore me.

meditations.body:
Scripture never shows the Risen Christ meeting His Mother —
and never shows her at the tomb with the spice-bearers either.
She is the one person in Jerusalem not looking for a body.
The saints have held, by an old and widespread conviction,
that He came to her first, before the garden, before anyone;
and the Church's Easter song to her assumes the meeting:
Queen of heaven, rejoice — for He whom thou wast worthy to bear has risen
as He said.
As He said. She is greeted with her own faith kept.
Rest in that room for a while: no words recorded, none needed —
the bride's line says it all.
I held him, and I will not let him go.

scripture.text: Jesus saith to her: Mary. She turning, saith to him: Rabboni (which is to say, Master).

meditations.body:
She is looking straight at Him and cannot see Him —
grief has decided already what is possible, and He does not fit inside it.
Then one word: Mary.
Recognition arrives not through her eyes but through her name,
spoken the way only one voice had ever said it.
The Church has always smiled at her mistake,
because she was wrong and exactly right: He is the gardener —
the new Adam, in a garden, at dawn, undoing what the first gardener let die.
He still tends to be recognized this way:
not when we finally see clearly, but when we hear ourselves named.

scripture.text: Then cometh Simon Peter, following him, and went into the sepulchre: and saw the linen cloths lying, And the napkin that had been about his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but apart, wrapped up into one place.

meditations.body:
No thief wraps the napkin and sets it apart.
Whatever left this tomb left it in order.

scripture.text: And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?

meditations.body:
His first words to the assembled Church are not a commission but a question:
why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?
He has walked through a locked door to ask it,
and He has been asking it through locked doors ever since.
The troubles were real — they had watched Him die.
The Resurrection did not scold the fear;
it stood in the middle of the fear and outweighed it.
So take His question as addressed, tonight, to the room you have locked:
which of your standing troubles has this morning already answered —
if you let it?

scripture.text: Jesus saith to him: Because thou hast seen me, Thomas, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen and have believed.

meditations.body:
He kept the wounds.
A glorified body could have been unmarked, and His is not —
here is why: He shows them to His Father in all their beauty,
as titles to the communication of His grace,
ever living to make intercession for us.
The scars are not evidence of damage survived;
they are credentials, presented in heaven on your behalf at this hour.
And to Thomas, with a hand in those credentials,
He speaks the Gospel's last beatitude —
blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed —
aimed straight past Thomas at everyone who would ever pray this decade.
You are the person that sentence was for.

scripture.text: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and so, to enter into his glory?

meditations.body:
On the Emmaus road He asks the question that joins the Sorrowful mysteries
to the Glorious: ought not Christ to have suffered these things,
and so to enter into his glory?
Ought not — the cross was never the plan failing.
Then He does for two discouraged walkers what this whole devotion does:
beginning at Moses, He reads His own story through all the Scriptures,
and their hearts burn without their knowing why.
They recognize Him at last in the breaking of bread —
and He vanishes, because from now on that is where He will be held.
Whoever has left Mass unable to say what happened, only that something did,
has walked this road.

scripture.text: Therefore if you be risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God.

meditations.body:
Do not let the mystery stay in the past tense.
He left the linen cloths in the tomb as the symbol of our infirmities
and imperfections — and the font of baptism, Paul teaches,
is the figure of that sepulchre: buried with Him there,
we came up out of the water to walk in newness of life.
The Resurrection is not only something that happened to Him;
sacramentally, it has already happened to you.
The verse draws the consequence: if you be risen with Christ,
seek the things that are above.
Live like someone whose grave is behind him.

scripture.text: Knowing that Christ, rising again from the dead, dieth now no more. Death shall no more have dominion over him.

meditations.body:
Others had come back from death before this morning —
the widow's son, Jairus's daughter, Lazarus still wearing his grave clothes.
Every one of them came back on loan, through the same door twice,
and the door closed behind them again in the end.
Paul marks what makes this morning categorically different:
Christ rising again from the dead, dieth now no more;
death shall no more have dominion over him.
Not a reprieve — a release.
Not the door reopened, but the door taken off its hinges.
Everyone raised before Him returned to mortal life.
He rose out the far side of death itself, and He holds the exit open.

scripture.text: And when I had seen him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying: Fear not. I am the First and the Last, And alive, and was dead. And behold I am living for ever and ever and have the keys of death and of hell.

meditations.body:
When John sees Him in glory and falls at His feet as dead,
the Risen One identifies Himself by His history: I was dead —
and behold I am living for ever and ever,
and have the keys of death and of hell.
The icon paints the claim: gates broken flat, locks scattered,
Adam and Eve pulled up by the wrist.
He does not pick death's lock; He owns the keys.
So one question to carry out of the decade:
what door are you still guarding as if the keys were yours?
He has them. Hand Him yours.

scripture.text: Behold my beloved speaketh to me: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning is come: the voice of the turtle is heard in our land:

meditations.body:
Read the Bridegroom's spring-call to the soul, and name the winter:
the torpor of acedia, the cold of envy,
the rain the din of clamoring thoughts.
Then the thaw — flowers in the land —
the virtues breaking out in the field of the heart,
a field that is mine and thine at once.
As the rising sun scatters fog, so the Sun of wisdom entering a soul drives
out the torpor, stills the anger, gladdens everything.
And one warning, gentle and serious:
the golden hour of His visitation is not to be neglected.
Easter is knocking on the interior life too.
Rise, make haste.

scripture.text: This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein.

meditations.body:
For a full octave the Church sings one verse as if time had stopped:
this is the day which the Lord hath made —
one day, eight days long, because Easter would not fit inside a single
sunrise.
And then she kept going: every Sunday since has been this day again,
a little Easter, week upon week until the end of the world.
Which means the decade does not end by leaving the mystery;
it ends inside it.
Today — whatever the calendar says, whatever kind of day it has been —
is still the day the Lord hath made.
She rejoiced in it first, greeted by her risen Son.
Let us be glad and rejoice therein.

scripture.text: And he had in his right hand seven stars. And from his mouth came out a sharp two-edged sword. And his face was as the sun shineth in his power.

meditations.body:
End, this time, without an idea.
John saw the risen Face and wrote down what he could:
his face was as the sun shineth in his power.
You have gazed at this Face twice before in these mysteries —
crowned and bandaged in the praetorium, pierced and still on Calvary.
Now finish the gazing where it was always going:
the same Face, unbound, alight, looking back at you with nothing in between.
Do not analyse the decade. Do not summarize it.
For the last ten Hail Marys, only look —
and let yourself be someone the risen Christ is glad to see.

scripture.text: And he led them out as far as Bethania: and lifting up his hands, he blessed them.

meditations.body:
The last thing His feet do on earth is walk.
He leads them out as far as Bethany —
the same road past Gethsemani, up the same Mount of Olives where He sweat
blood — and this time the climb ends not in arrest but in blessing.
Forty days He has been appearing and vanishing;
now He walks somewhere with them one more time, at walking pace,
the way the whole thing began by the lakeshore.
Climb the hill with the eleven for this decade.
He is in no hurry, and the view from the top is about to change forever.

scripture.text: God is ascended with jubilee, and the Lord with the sound of trumpet.

meditations.body: The psalter had the trumpet ready a thousand years in advance.

scripture.text: And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sitteth on the right hand of God.

meditations.body:
Venture the claim: of all the feasts of Our Lord,
the Ascension is in a certain sense the greatest —
the supreme glorification of Christ.
The Resurrection was the dawn of that glory;
the Ascension is its full noontide.
And the visible ascent the apostles watched is itself only the symbol
of an ascension they could not see: above all the heavens,
past every choir of angels, stopping nowhere short of the right hand of God.
What the eye followed for a few seconds, faith follows all the way up.

scripture.text: Which he wrought in Christ, raising him up from the dead and setting him on his right hand in the heavenly places. Above all principality and power and virtue and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come.

meditations.body:
Seated at the right hand: be careful about both words.
The right hand is a figure — God is spirit, and has no right or left —
but Scripture keeps the phrase to say what nothing else could:
the sublimity of the triumph granted to Christ in the sanctuary
of the divinity.
And seated does not mean idle.
It means He has entered forever into the repose His combats merited —
a rest that does not exclude the continual exercise of the omnipotence
by which He rules, sanctifies, and judges.
He is not resting from the work. He is reigning in it.

scripture.text: And it came to pass, whilst he blessed them, he departed from them and was carried up to heaven.

meditations.body:
Watch the grammar of the verse: whilst he blessed them, he departed.
Not after.
The blessing was still in motion when the ground let Him go —
hands raised over them, the words perhaps still coming —
and Luke never says the blessing ended.
The last sight anyone on earth had of the mortal-born Christ is His hands
lifted in benediction over the people He loved.
The Church has lived ever since inside that unfinished gesture.
So do you.
Whatever else this decade holds, hold this:
the posture He left in is the posture He holds still.

scripture.text: Who also said: Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven? This Jesus who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you have seen him going into heaven.

meditations.body:
Two men in white with a gentle question: why stand you looking up to heaven?
The gazing was right — for a moment.
But the angels interrupt it because standing and looking was about to become
a way of life, and there was a world to be told.
Contemplation that never turns and walks back down the hill curdles into
nostalgia.
So take their question personally, since it was preserved for you:
where in your life has looking up become standing still —
a devotion, a grief, a waiting that was holy once and is now the reason you
have not moved?

scripture.text: Jesus saith to her: Do not touch me: for I am not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brethren and say to them: I ascend to my Father and to your Father, to my God and to your God.

meditations.body: Four possessives in one sentence, and two of them are yours.

scripture.text: He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even to the death of the cross. For which cause, God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names:

meditations.body:
Why this incommensurable glory? Two reasons.
First, He is God's own Son: the Humanity seated on high is the Humanity
of a God, and divine glory is its birthright —
veiled through the mortal years, glimpsed once on Thabor;
the risen body needed an abode that answered its condition,
and only heaven would do.
Second, it is recompense: He had said behold, I come to do thy will,
and drank the abasement to the dregs — for which cause God hath exalted him.
You met that arc at the crowning with thorns.
This is where it lands.

scripture.text: Wherefore he saith: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive: he gave gifts to men.

meditations.body:
He did not go up alone.
On the day of espousals Christ ascended carrying His spoils with Him —
the souls of the Saints He had led out of limbo, brought up in His train.
Adam and Eve, the patriarchs, the prophets,
the good thief a few weeks into paradise:
the procession the Anastasis icon began, the Ascension completes.
Paul had found it in the psalm: ascending on high, he led captivity captive.
The first human beings to enter heaven entered it that day, behind Him,
because of Him — and the road they took has never been closed since.

scripture.text: Which we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm, and which entereth in even within the veil: Where the forerunner Jesus is entered for us, made a high priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.

meditations.body:
Hebrews reaches for a sailor's image: hope as an anchor of the soul —
but thrown upward, entering in even within the veil,
where the forerunner Jesus is entered for us.
An anchor holds from where it lands, not from where it was thrown.
If yours is fastened inside the veil,
then the line between you and heaven is already taut,
and the storms here can toss the boat without moving the mooring.
He is called forerunner: the one who goes ahead specifically so that others
can follow.
Nobody runs ahead on a road no one else will travel.
The word itself is a promise.

scripture.text: But our conversation is in heaven: from whence also we look for the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ,

meditations.body:
Find the grace of the feast where the Church always hides it, in the collect:
grant that we who believe Thy Son this day ascended into heaven may
ourselves also dwell there in spirit — mente in caelestibus habitemus.
Not visit. Dwell.
The Ascension is not only His change of address; it is meant to be yours:
a life lived here, at this desk, in this kitchen,
with the heart already keeping house above.
Paul says it flatly: our conversation is in heaven.
Citizenship, the word means.
You are praying this decade abroad.

scripture.text: But I tell you the truth: it is expedient to you that I go. For if I go not, the Paraclete will not come to you: but if I go, I will send him to you.

meditations.body:
It is expedient to you that I go.
It cannot have sounded true on the night He said it,
and the Ascension is where it becomes arithmetic.
While He walked in Galilee, to be with Him you had to be in Galilee —
one province, one crowd, one conversation at a time.
Seated in glory, He is bound to no road and no hour:
present to every soul at once, nearer to you now than He was to the crowds
who touched His cloak.
And a footnote worth a lifetime adds:
He dwells also by the Real Presence in the Sacrament.
He did not leave the earth when He left the hill.

scripture.text: All these were persevering with one mind in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.

meditations.body:
Her last appearance in Scripture is one clause:
persevering with one mind in prayer, with Mary the mother of Jesus.
Fill in what the clause holds: after the Ascension she willingly remained,
understanding it to be God's will for the good of the Church —
resolving the disciples' doubts, comforting them under persecution,
spurring them on.
Willingly — though where your treasure is, there is your heart,
and hers was wholly above.
The paradox lives in four Latin words: Mariae cella fuit coelum.
The cell of Mary was heaven.
She stayed below for decades and never once lived anywhere else.

scripture.text: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.

meditations.body:
He tied the promise to the leaving:
behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world —
spoken on the mountain of departure, in the same breath as goodbye.
The apostles learned to hold both: gone from sight, with them always,
and the second truer than the first.
Most of us have an absence we are still grieving as pure loss.
So let the mystery ask its question plainly:
where in your life might an absence be a mode of His presence you have
not yet recognized — the door He went through not to leave you,
but to be with you differently?

scripture.text: And they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy. And they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

meditations.body:
The strangest joy in the Gospels: He leaves,
and they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy.
No tears on the road down.
They had finally understood who had been with them and where He now sits —
and understood that His going up was not subtraction but coronation,
theirs as much as His.
Luke ends his whole Gospel on the next clause:
they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God.
That is the way down from every mountain of prayer,
and it is the way out of this decade:
back into the city, glad, with the blessing still unfinished overhead.

mysteries.title: The Descent of the Holy Spirit

scripture.text: And when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place:

meditations.body:
Between the hill of the Ascension and this morning lie ten days about which
Scripture records almost nothing except the one thing that matters:
they waited.
He had told them not to depart from Jerusalem but to wait for the promise
of the Father — and the Church has always counted those ten days as her first
novena: the original nine-days'-prayer, made before the word existed,
by the people who invented Christian waiting.
Whatever you have been asking God for through this rosary,
you are standing in their room.
The instruction has not changed. Wait for the promise.

scripture.text: Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth.

meditations.body:
The Church still asks this in the present tense, every Pentecost,
as if the face of the earth were not yet finished being renewed.
It is not.

scripture.text: Going therefore, teach ye all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost.

meditations.body:
Who is it that came?
Enter the sanctuary of the Trinity to answer:
the Father, principle without principle; the Son, His perfect Word and image;
and from their mutual gift of self proceeds the Holy Spirit —
the final term of the divine communications.
Love between the first two Persons, in Person.
Concerning these things we can but lisp —
and yet Jesus revealed them on the eve of His death, to His friends,
that our joy may be filled.
What descended on the cenacle is the love God is.

scripture.text: Now this he said of the Spirit which they should receive who believed in him: for as yet the Spirit was not given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.

meditations.body:
John says something easy to read past:
the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
The order could not be otherwise: the gift of the Spirit, like every grace,
was merited by Jesus — it is the fruit of His Passion;
He purchased it by the sufferings He endured.
Divine Love in Person, bought at the price you spent five decades
contemplating in the Sorrowful mysteries.
Pentecost is not a new project of God's;
it is Calvary's harvest, ten days after the Sower went home.
The fire over each head was paid for.

scripture.text: And the angel answering, said to her: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee. And therefore also the Holy which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.

meditations.body:
One person in that upper room had felt this before.
The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, Gabriel had said in Nazareth,
and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee —
and now, thirty-three years later, the same Spirit descends on the same
woman, in a room full of frightened men she has been mothering for ten days.
The first overshadowing formed the body of Christ within her.
This one forms the mystical body of Christ around her.
She is the hinge between the two — the only soul present at both comings,
praying at the center of the room the way the icons have always painted her.
Rest there beside her while the fire falls.

scripture.text: All these were persevering with one mind in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.

meditations.body:
Notice the word order of the verse and do not let it go:
Luke names the apostles, then the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus last.
Not because Luke forgot who she was —
but because she had taken the lowest place in the room, after everyone,
and Luke simply recorded where people sat.
Then the verdict: justly has the last become first, who,
when she was first of all, became last.
The same woman was absent from Palm Sunday's applause and present
on Calvary's hill of disgrace.
She had a lifelong policy about crowds and honor.
It held in the cenacle too.

scripture.text: And there appeared to them parted tongues, as it were of fire: and it sat upon every one of them.

meditations.body: The flame parted so that everyone in the room could have some.

scripture.text: And suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming: and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.

meditations.body:
Notice where the wind goes: it filled the whole house where they were
sitting.
They were indoors — the same kind of room they had locked for fear since
Easter, the hiding place of a movement that had not yet moved.
The Spirit does not stand outside the door waiting for them to find courage
and come out.
He fills the hiding place itself, floor to ceiling,
until the building cannot hold what is in it and the door opens from
the inside.
If your own faith currently lives behind a locked door somewhere,
take the verse literally.
He is willing to start in there.

scripture.text: And when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded in mind, because that every man heard them speak in his own tongue.

meditations.body:
The Church has always read this morning against Babel.
There, one proud tongue was shattered into many and the peoples scattered;
here the many tongues remain — and every man hears the wonders of God
in his own.
The Spirit does not repeal Babel by restoring a single language;
He does something better: unity without uniformity,
one Gospel wearing every mother tongue on earth.
The miracle was not that the crowd learned Galilean.
It was that no one had to stop being who they were to hear God speak
to them.
The Church was catholic — universal — from her first sentence.

scripture.text: But the Paraclete, the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring all things to your mind, whatsoever I shall have said to you.

meditations.body:
Another Paraclete, Jesus had promised —
and the apostles were to find in Him another Himself.
Not a substitute teacher with different lessons:
the same Teacher, moved inside.
He will teach you all things, and bring all things to your mind,
whatsoever I shall have said to you —
the Spirit as the memory of the Church,
the one who makes three years of half-understood words suddenly cohere.
Every time a Gospel line you have heard a hundred times abruptly opens
and reads you instead, that promise is being kept.
The Teacher did not leave the classroom.
He entered the students.

scripture.text: But Peter standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and spoke to them: Ye men of Judea, and all you that dwell in Jerusalem, be this known to you and with your ears receive my words.

meditations.body:
But Peter standing up.
Three words, and a resurrection inside them.
The last time Peter faced a hostile audience it was one servant girl
by a fire, and he broke three times before the rooster finished.
Now he stands before thousands in the city that executed his Lord seven
weeks ago, raises his voice, and preaches the first homily of the Church —
and three thousand souls are baptized by nightfall.
Same man. Same weakness, presumably, somewhere underneath.
New wind.
Courage is the Spirit's signature gift, and He gives it, as at Pentecost,
precisely to people with a documented history of collapse.

scripture.text: For the Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world: and that which containeth all things, hath knowledge of the voice.

meditations.body:
The mystery's largest claim fits in three words: Pentecost ever continues.
The assembly in the cenacle represents the entire Church —
and the Spirit's action in her is wonderful and unceasing.
The fire of Acts is the permanent weather of the Church:
every sacrament on every altar this morning.
The Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world —
present tense in the verse, present tense still.
You did not miss Pentecost by twenty centuries.
You are inside it.

scripture.text: Likewise, the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity. For, we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings,

meditations.body:
Paul reveals what may be the Spirit's most hidden work:
when we do not know what to pray, the Spirit himself asketh for us
with unspeakable groanings — prayer happening in you, beneath you,
when you have no words at all.
Which reframes every prayer you have ever abandoned for lack of language.
So let the question of this decade be gentle:
what have you stopped praying about because you could not find the words —
and what if the wordlessness itself, the ache that has no sentence,
was the Spirit already praying it better than your words ever did?

scripture.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, Mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity. Against such there is no law.

meditations.body:
Wind, fire, and tongues were the launch; the cargo is quieter.
Paul inventories what the Spirit actually produces where He dwells:
charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness,
faith, modesty, continency, chastity.
Fruit — which grows slowly, in season, and mostly without the tree noticing.
So read the list once more, unhurried, as the decade's question:
which of these has quietly grown in you this past year that you never
planted and cannot take credit for?
Find it, name it, and know that you have located the Holy Ghost at work
in your own life.

scripture.text: And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles and in the communication of the breaking of bread and in prayers.

meditations.body:
Luke tells us how the first day of the Church ended:
three thousand new souls, persevering in the doctrine of the apostles,
and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Teaching, Eucharist, prayer — the whole shape of Catholic life,
assembled before sunset on day one, and never since disassembled.
The fire became a community; the wind became a way of living.
And notice where the sentence lands: in prayers.
The Church's first day ended the way your decade is ending now.
From their upper room to yours — same Spirit, same fire,
still parting so that everyone can have some.

scripture.text: Arise, O Lord, into thy resting place: thou and the ark, which thou hast sanctified.

meditations.body:
From here to the end of the Rosary, Scripture falls silent:
no evangelist recorded this mystery.
But history left a silence of its own that speaks almost as loudly.
The early Church collected the bones of her martyrs and built altars over
them — yet no city on earth has ever claimed the body of the Mother of God.
Not Jerusalem, not Ephesus, no one.
The one relic all Christendom would have fought over does not exist,
and the Church has always known why.
The psalm had asked for it: arise, O Lord, into thy resting place —
thou, and the ark which thou hast sanctified.

scripture.text: But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.

meditations.body:
How did she spend the years of waiting?
The old tradition relates it: she went on pilgrimage through her own
memories — the stable at Bethlehem, the workshop at Nazareth,
the garden of Gethsemani, the hall of the scourging,
the place of the crowning, and most often Calvary and the holy sepulchre.
Station by station, she walked what you are praying.
The woman who kept all these words in her heart spent her last years
visiting them.
You are not performing a devotion she would find foreign.
You are keeping her habit.

scripture.text: And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?

meditations.body:
But the holy places could not satisfy
her, because her heart could not find its rest on this earth at all.
Put David's sighs on her lips, with more ardent love than David's:
who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest —
and the hart panting for the fountains of water.
Hers was the purest homesickness that ever existed:
not weariness of earth, but love of Someone in particular who was elsewhere.
She had a treasure, and where the treasure is, the heart is also.
For thirty-some years, her heart lived at an address her feet could
not reach.

scripture.text: And Mary said: Behold the handmaid of the Lord: be it done to me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.

meditations.body:
Then, as the old historians gather it, Gabriel came back —
the same angel, with a second annunciation:
prepare to leave the earth; come take possession of thy kingdom,
for all its citizens await thee.
And what did she answer?
The same four words as the first time, at Nazareth, when she was fifteen:
behold the handmaid of the Lord.
Ecce ancilla Domini.
She received the summons to glory in exactly the posture in which she had
received the summons to motherhood.
First fiat: the Incarnation.
Second, at the Presentation: the offering.
This is the third, and the word has not changed.
It never needed to.

scripture.text: After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own.

meditations.body:
Her tenderest farewell was for John —
the son given her from the cross, who had kept her for thirty years.
Hear what the tradition remembers her saying to him:
My John, I thank thee for all thy care of me.
If I leave thee now, I am going to pray for thee.
Do not forget me; in all thy necessities call me to thy aid,
for I never will forget thee, my beloved son.
Read that again slowly, because from that hour the disciple took
her to his own — and the disciple is you.
Her deathbed promise to John is her standing promise to everyone he stands
for: call me, in all of them.
I never will forget thee.

scripture.text: Put me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy as hard as hell, the lamps thereof are fire and flames.

meditations.body:
What did she die of?
The Fathers and Doctors generally affirm that she died of no infirmity
at all: she died of pure love.
A rule was laid down
for her: Mary either ought not to die, or die only of love.
The divine fire that had burned in her since Nazareth simply finished
its work — the celestial phoenix, losing her life in the midst of that flame.
You have met the verse before, at the foot of the cross, as a wound:
love is strong as death.
Here it is again as a victory.
In her, love and death met a final time — and it was death that gave way.

scripture.text: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I languish with love.

meditations.body:
The angels filled the room, and she sent them back for her Son.
Even heaven's court is not heaven.

scripture.text: Behold my beloved speaketh to me: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

meditations.body:
Then Jesus Himself came for her — with the cross in His hand.
Why the cross, at a joyful deathbed?
To show the glory He had won by it:
having by His death made the acquisition of this great creature.
The cross at her bedside is the receipt —
everything this hour holds was purchased there.
And the icon of the mystery answers with its own reversal:
Christ standing over her bed, holding her soul in His arms like a swaddled
child.
The Madonna and Child, at last, the other way around.

scripture.text: The daughters of kings have delighted thee in thy glory. The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing; surrounded with variety.

meditations.body:
Hear what heaven said as she arrived.
The Canticle asks it: who is this that cometh up from the desert,
flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? —
and this all the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem could have cried
at the Assumption of the glorious Virgin, astonished beyond measure:
for then she leaned most fully upon her Beloved,
who led her out of this valley of tears to such surpassing glory,
placing her above the whole army of heaven.
Every previous arrival had been a rescued soul.
This one came up the road leaning on the King's own arm —
and heaven, which is not easily surprised, asked who is this.
The queen stood at His right hand.

scripture.text: But now Christ is risen from the dead, the firstfruits of them that sleep:

meditations.body:
Be precise about what the Church actually teaches here,
because the precision is the glory: Mary was assumed body and soul.
Not her spirit released from flesh —
the whole woman, the body that carried God, taken entire into glory.
Christ rose as the firstfruits of them that sleep;
she is the first fruit of the firstfruits:
the first of the merely redeemed to arrive complete,
the proof that His Resurrection was not a private privilege but a door held
open.
What He is by right, she is by gift —
and what she is by gift, you are promised.
The exit He tore in death, somebody has now walked through.
Your body's future exists, and it is standing in heaven.

scripture.text: Thou art all fair, O my love, and there is not a spot in thee.

meditations.body: Death searched her and found nothing it could keep.

scripture.text: As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God.

meditations.body:
Her whole last season on earth was homesickness —
not for a place but for a Person; she missed Someone.
Which puts a quiet question to the way most of us hold heaven:
as a comfort filed away for later, a destination assumed rather than
desired.
She ached for it the way the hart pants for water,
because she knew exactly whom it contained.
So ask yourself, gently, inside this decade:
is your heaven a place you expect, or a Person you already miss?
And if the longing is faint — she is proof it can be prayed into flame,
one mystery at a time, the way she fed hers at Bethlehem and Calvary.

scripture.text: And the temple of God was opened in heaven: and the ark of his testament was seen in his temple. And there were lightnings and voices and an earthquake and great hail.

meditations.body:
The decade opened with a psalm's petition: arise, O Lord, into thy rest —
thou and the ark.
Here is the petition answered, in the last book of the Bible:
the temple of God was opened in heaven,
and the ark of his testament was seen in his temple.
John looks through the opened door and sees the ark —
not lost, not captured, not crumbled in some cave, but home.
The Church has always recognized her in that verse:
the living ark, gold within and without, who carried the Word, the Manna,
and the true High Priest.
What Israel lost and mourned, heaven displays.
The Assumption is the ark procession arriving,
and the whole temple open to show it.

scripture.text: And the wine failing, the mother of Jesus saith to him: They have no wine.

meditations.body:
In all thy necessities call me to thy aid.
That was her deathbed instruction to John — and through him, to you.
Her style of intercession has been on record since Cana:
she does not lecture her Son or negotiate; she states the need —
they have no wine — and lets Him be Himself about it.
So the mystery's question is the most practical one in this whole Rosary:
when did you last actually do it?
Not admire her, not think warmly of her —
call her, by name, about a specific necessity.
You began tonight with intentions.
Choose the heaviest one and hand it to the woman who said I never will
forget thee, and see what she does with the wine.

scripture.text: Thou hast made known to me the ways of life, thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance: at thy right hand are delights even to the end.

meditations.body:
At the empty tomb she had held Him and said I will not let him go —
and then let Him go, for thirty more years of exile.
This hour ends the letting.
The face she searched Jerusalem for as a girl, the face they bandaged,
the face she watched go grey on the cross, the face as the sun in his power:
hers now, forever, at arm's length that never lengthens again.
Thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance.
And every night since, the Church has ended the Hail Mary with the hour she
now knows from the inside: pray for us sinners,
now and at the hour of our death.
Say tonight's last one slowly.
She has been through that door, body and soul — and she is holding it.

scripture.text: And a great sign appeared in heaven: A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.

meditations.body:
The Bible's last portrait of her is its most tremendous:
a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet,
and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
The girl nobody in Nazareth looked at twice is now a great sign appearing
in heaven.
Nothing about her changed — that is the point of the whole Rosary you have
prayed: the handmaid was always this; glory has only made it visible.
Begin the final mystery by holding the two pictures at once:
the small room where an angel found her, and the sky she now wears.
The distance between them is what God does with a yes.

scripture.text: He hath put down the mighty from their seat and hath exalted the humble.

meditations.body:
She announced the mechanism of this day herself, at Elizabeth's door,
thirty years before Calvary and an eternity before the crown.

scripture.text: Then Bethsabee came to king Solomon, to speak to him for Adonias: and the king arose to meet her, and bowed to her, and sat down upon his throne: and a throne was set for the king’s mother, and she sat on his right hand. And she said to him: I desire one small petition of thee; do not put me to confusion. And the king said to her: My mother ask, for I must not turn away thy face.

meditations.body:
Her queenship is not the Church's sentiment;
it is the constitution of David's kingdom.
In Israel the queen was never the king's wife — kings had many —
but always his mother, the Gebirah.
Watch Solomon receive Bathsheba: the king rises to meet her, bows,
and has a throne set for the king's mother at his right hand.
Then the words every Hail Mary relies
on: ask, my mother, for I must not turn away thy face.
Gabriel said her Son would receive the throne of David his father.
He did — and David's throne comes with a second seat,
and a standing rule about the mother's requests.

scripture.text: God hath spoken once, these two things have I heard, that power belongeth to God, And mercy to thee, O Lord; for thou wilt render to every man according to his works.

meditations.body:
A daring piece of arithmetic opens this mystery.
David had heard two things: that power belongeth to God, and mercy to thee,
O Lord.
The kingdom of God consists of justice and mercy —
and the Lord has divided it: the kingdom of justice He reserved for Himself,
and the kingdom of mercy He granted to Mary,
ordaining that the mercies dispensed to men should pass through her hands.
Take the claim slowly.
Not that she has mercy of her own apart from God —
but that He chose to give His through a mother,
because He knows how His children take medicine.

scripture.text: Give to the king thy judgment, O God, and to the king’s son thy justice: To judge thy people with justice, and thy poor with judgment.

meditations.body:
Stack the witnesses.
When she conceived and bore the Word,
she obtained the half of the kingdom of God —
queen of mercy, Christ remaining king of justice.
To the Son the office of judging; to the mother the office
of compassionating the wretched.
And a saint dared to improve a psalm: give to the king thy judgment, O God —
and to his mother thy mercy.
If the audacity makes you flinch, remember who arranged it.
The Son crowned her; the saints are only reading the coronation's terms
aloud.

scripture.text: And the king said to her: What wilt thou, queen Esther? what is thy request? if thou shouldst even ask one half of the kingdom, it shall be given to thee.

meditations.body:
A type from Scripture seals the divided kingdom: Queen Esther.
A decree of death stood against her whole people;
she entered the throne room unbidden, at the risk of her life —
and the king held out the sceptre and said the words exactly:
though thou ask the half of my kingdom.
A condemned people, a queen who is one of them,
a king who cannot refuse her face: the Book of Esther is the Coronation
drawn in advance.
The decree against us still stands written somewhere.
So does she, at the throne, unbidden by anyone but love.

scripture.text: Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes, and with one hair of thy neck.

meditations.body:
The strangest line in the Canticle — turn away thy eyes from me —
is the speech of a lover overcome.
Christ says it to His own Mother as amorous hyperbole:
He has already told her thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes —
how much more with both?
He cannot bear her gaze for the wound of love it deals Him.
And then the clause that stops the breath:
those dove-like, contemplative eyes of hers drew me from the bosom
of the Father into thy womb.
In the order of love, her gaze caused the Incarnation.
Heaven's King is, by His own account, a conquered man.

scripture.text: Turn away thy eyes from me, for they have made me flee away. Thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from Galaad.

meditations.body:
Then the verse yields its second meaning,
and it is the charter of her reign.
Turn thy eyes from me, Christ tells His crowned Mother, means this:
those eyes of maternal compassion and loving care which thou hadst on me
on earth — passible, mortal, above all in the time of the Passion —
turn them now wholly from me, fully glorified,
and turn them to the wretched exiles crying out to thee:
Eia ergo, Advocata nostra — turn then, our Advocate,
those thy merciful eyes toward us.
Read that again: the Salve Regina's petition, in the mouth of Christ,
as her coronation assignment.
The Church has spent centuries begging her to do what her Son commissioned
in the same words.
I no longer need those eyes, He says. They do.

scripture.text: All the glory of the king’s daughter is within in golden borders,

meditations.body:
Now stop, and only watch.
The hands that were nailed lift a crown;
the head that wore thorns bends toward hers;
the same two faces that met on the Via Dolorosa meet over a diadem.
She receives it the way she has received everything since Nazareth —
asking nothing, adding nothing, all the glory of the king's daughter within.
Do not draw a lesson from this decade.
There is no assignment.
The Son is crowning His Mother, and you were brought here to see it —
a child at a coronation, allowed in because you are family.
For ten Hail Marys, be nothing but glad.

scripture.text: And thou shalt be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.

meditations.body:
Isaias supplies the mystery's secret:
thou shalt be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord.
She is crowned — and she is herself a crown, held in His hand,
made of the redemption's first and perfect fruit.
And her own crown, the twelve stars:
the tribes, the apostles, the whole gathered People —
which is to say, the jewels in her diadem are the redeemed.
A queen's glory is her people.
Her coronation is not a promotion away from us;
it is her being fastened to us forever,
the way a crown is fastened to what it honors.
You are somewhere in the setting, and she does not intend to lose a stone.

scripture.text: I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel.

meditations.body:
The first promise in Scripture and its last portrait are the same woman.
The serpent waited the whole Bible to lose.

scripture.text: Behold as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, As the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress: so are our eyes unto the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us.

meditations.body:
If mercy truly passes through her hands,
the psalm has already taught the posture:
as the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress,
so are our eyes on the Lord.
Eyes on the hands — watching for what is given, and through whom.
Which raises a question worth an honest answer:
are you willing to receive grace secondhand?
Some souls will take from God only what arrives direct,
no mother in the middle, no mediation they didn't choose.
But He built the kingdom with her hands in it.
This week, ask for one specific grace explicitly through her —
and watch the hands.

scripture.text: In the vale of tears, in the place which he hath set.

meditations.body:
You have known the Coronation's theology by heart for years,
because it is the Salve Regina.
Hail, holy Queen — the crown.
Mother of mercy — the handed-over half of the kingdom.
Mourning and weeping in this valley of tears —
the psalm's own phrase for the exile she watches.
Turn then, most gracious Advocate, thine eyes of mercy toward us —
the commission her Son gave her, word for word.
And the last petition tells you what kind of queen she
is: after this our exile, show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
Her final act, every time, is to point away from herself.
The prayer ends on His name because she insists on it.

scripture.text: The four and twenty ancients fell down before him that sitteth on the throne and adored him that liveth for ever and ever and cast their crowns before the throne, saying:

meditations.body:
The word Rosary means a garland — a crown of roses woven for the Queen,
one Ave per rose.
Which means you have not merely been meditating tonight;
you have been making something, and it is finished, and it is in your hands.
In heaven the elders cast their crowns before the throne;
she lays hers there too, first and gladdest of all.
So the last question of the Glorious mysteries is simply this:
what did you weave this crown for?
Take the intentions you named at the beginning — the people, the burdens —
set them among the roses, and lay the whole thing at her feet,
to be carried where she carries everything.

scripture.text: His mother saith to the waiters: Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.

meditations.body:
The Rosary's twenty mysteries end here, at her coronation —
so let her have the last word, and notice which one she chose.
Scripture records her final sentence at a wedding feast,
spoken to servants who did not know what was coming:
whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.
That is the only instruction she ever gave,
and she has never issued another.
Crowned above the angels, holding half the kingdom,
with the King unable to turn away her face —
everything she has, she spends on pointing at Him.
So go the way she sends everyone: back down from the vision,
into the kitchen and the water jars, doing whatsoever He says.
The Queen's whole reign is in that sentence.
The rest is roses.
